rewritten_text:
My father had been the life within my life, and now his memory held that place. I could feel gratitude toward someone else, but I could never again love or hope as I once had. Everything was suffering; even pleasure was something I endured rather than enjoyed. I resembled a lonely hollow in the mountains, enclosed on every side by steep black cliffs, beyond the reach of warmth and without a path to sunnier fields. That was why the spirit of friendship could soothe me briefly but could not restore me. It arrived like a gentle visitation, and when it left I scarcely felt its absence. The spirit of life was dead inside me. Do not be surprised, then, that I welcomed heaven's finest gift—a friend—with so little joy, or mourned its departure with so little bitterness.

My friend's name was Woodville. I will briefly tell his story, so that you may understand how cold my heart must have grown to resist the warmth of his eloquence and tender sympathy. Since he too was profoundly unhappy, we might have consoled each other well, had the Medusa head of Misery not turned me to stone. Woodville's misfortunes had not struck at the heart's very core as mine had. His grief was natural, capable of purifying rather than destroying the heart. Once its shadow lifted, he might emerge brighter and happier than before.

Woodville was the son of a poor clergyman and had received a classical education. He belonged to that rare handful whom fortune favours from birth, showering them without restraint with gifts of mind and body, and guarding them so closely that no imperfection, however slight, or disappointment, however brief, is allowed to touch them. She seemed to have made his mind from a substance so excellent that no impurity could stain it, and his understanding so sound that no error could distort it. His genius was extraordinary. When it rose like a brilliant star in the east, every eye turned toward it in admiration. He was a poet, though that name has been so often degraded that it cannot express everything he was. He resembled one of the ancient poets, crowned by the Muses in his cradle, with bees feeding upon his lips. Among other men he seemed surrounded by a heavenly radiance that set him apart and raised him above them. His exceptional beauty, the dazzling fire in his eyes, and the rich tones of his speech, which held listeners silent in ecstatic wonder, made him surpass everyone else. Before him, other people seemed created only to serve his superior excellence.

"Jupiter," he said when we reached the foot of the tree, "come here. Was the skull nailed to the branch facing outward or facing the wood?"

"Facing out, master, so the crows could get at the eyes easily."

"Then which eye did you drop the beetle through—this one or that one?" Legrand touched each of Jupiter's eyes in turn.

"This one, master—the left, just like you told me." But Jupiter pointed to his right eye.

"That's enough. We must try again."

My friend moved the peg marking where the beetle had landed about three inches west of its earlier position. I now saw, or thought I saw, some clear signs of a plan behind his madness. As before, he stretched the tape from the nearest point on the trunk to the peg, then continued straight out for fifty feet. The new spot was several yards away from the place where we had been digging.

He marked a slightly larger circle around this position, and we began digging again. I was terribly tired, but for reasons I could hardly understand, I no longer strongly resented the work. Somehow I had become interested—excited, even. Perhaps something in Legrand's strange behaviour suggested careful planning and thought, and that impressed me. I dug eagerly. Every so often I caught myself looking, almost hopefully, for the imaginary treasure whose promise had driven my unfortunate friend mad. At a moment when these strange thoughts had taken their strongest hold, and after perhaps an hour and a half of work, the dog's violent howling interrupted us again. Earlier, his restlessness had clearly come from playfulness or a passing whim. Now, however, his howls sounded fierce and serious. Jupiter tried once more to muzzle him, but he fought back furiously. Leaping into the hole, he clawed frantically at the earth. Within seconds he had exposed a pile of human bones making up two complete skeletons. Among them lay several metal buttons and what seemed to be the dusty remains of rotted woollen cloth. One or two blows of a spade turned up the blade of a large Spanish knife. As we dug farther, three or four loose gold and silver coins appeared.

Country folk, butchers, cattle-drivers, hawkers, boys, thieves, loafers, and vagabonds of every degraded sort crowded together in one mass. Drovers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and plunged, sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squealed; hawkers cried their wares amid shouting, swearing, and quarrels on every side. Bells rang and voices roared from each public-house. Everywhere there was pressing, shoving, driving, striking, whooping, and yelling. The dreadful, jarring clamour issuing from every part of the market, together with the filthy, unwashed, unshaven figures perpetually darting about and thrusting through the multitude, made a scene so deafening and bewildering that the senses were entirely overwhelmed.

Mr. Sikes hauled Oliver behind him as he forced a path through the densest part of the crowd, scarcely noticing the sights and noises that filled the boy with amazement. Two or three times he nodded to an acquaintance going by, and declined an equal number of invitations to a morning drink. He continued steadily until they had escaped the confusion and passed through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

"Now, youngster!" said Sikes, glancing at the clock on St. Andrew's Church. "Nearly seven! You'll have to move. Come along, Lazy-legs, don't start falling behind already!"

He reinforced these words with a sharp tug at his small companion's wrist. Oliver quickened into a sort of trot, midway between walking fast and running, and followed the house-breaker's long, hurried steps as best he could.

They maintained this speed until they had gone beyond Hyde Park Corner and were heading towards Kensington. Sikes then slowed until an empty cart, which had been following a little way behind, drew level. Noticing the name "Hounslow" upon it, he asked the driver, with all the politeness he could muster, to take them as far as Isleworth.

"Climb in," the man said. "Is that your lad?"

"Yes, my lad," Sikes answered, fixing Oliver with a hard stare and slipping his hand, seemingly absent-mindedly, into the pocket containing the pistol.

"Your father sets rather too fast a pace for you, doesn't he, young fellow?" asked the driver, noticing Oliver's breathlessness.

"Not at all," Sikes cut in. "He's accustomed to it. Here, Ned, catch my hand. Up you go!"

With this address to Oliver he lifted him into the cart. The driver indicated a pile of sacks and told the boy to stretch out and rest.

As milestone succeeded milestone, Oliver wondered increasingly where his companion intended to take him. They passed Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, yet continued as steadily as though their journey had only begun.
